claims.text: Thermal activation causes the metastable solid solution to evolve through nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
Mg-rich intermetallic compounds form both along grain boundaries and within the matrix.
Formation of Mg-rich intermetallics depletes Mg from the surrounding matrix.
Local Mg depletion inhibits formation of a continuous protective Mg-rich oxide layer.
Compositional inhomogeneities associated with the intermetallics promote localized galvanic corrosion.
The initial non-equilibrium metastable solid-solution state has homogeneously distributed elements.
Annealing at approximately 500–600 °C represents a service-relevant thermal treatment.
Enhanced diffusion at elevated temperature triggers nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallics.
Mg depletion caused by intermetallic formation limits formation of a stable protective oxide during high-temperature exposure.
Mg-rich intermetallic formation creates micro-galvanic cells that increase localized corrosion.
Thermally treated samples will have a higher volume fraction of fine Mg-rich intermetallics than the initial metastable state.
Thermally treated samples will have a less uniform Mg distribution than the initial metastable state.
Thermally treated samples will exhibit greater oxidation weight gain because their oxide scale is less protective.
Thermally treated samples will exhibit poorer corrosion resistance, including increased corrosion current density.
The initial metastable solid-solution state has inherently better oxidation and corrosion resistance than the annealed state.
The relevant service regime is above approximately 500 °C in oxygen-rich atmospheres and corrosive environments where protective-oxide integrity is critical.
